title: They Saved a UFO-Like Home From Demolition. Now It's Landing on the Market.
excerpt: Historic preservationist and former Obama appointee Milford Wayne Donaldson and his wife restored the plastic Futuro house.
content:
High in California’s San Jacinto Mountains near Idyllwild, a harvest-gold flying saucer is perched high on a large rock outcropping. 

The structure is a Futuro, a plastic home designed by the Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in the late 1960s. Of the estimated 100 Futuros made around the world, only about 50 or 60 are thought to remain, though there is no official accounting.

Located between Los Angeles and San Diego, the Futuro is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and as a California Historical Landmark. Now coming on the market for $1.495 million, the futuristic house has been the longtime passion project of Milford Wayne Donaldson, a preservation architect who was President Barack Obama’s appointee as chair of the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation. Milford, who goes by Wayne, and his wife, Laurie Donaldson, saved the Futuro from the wrecking ball and restored it. For years, the Donaldsons spent about a week a month at the Futuro, which has about 800 square feet of interior space and is a six-to-eight-hour drive from their primary home near Sacramento.

The Futuro is a throwback to a time when plastic was considered a wonder material—cheap, lightweight and very moldable, Wayne said. Popularized after World War II, plastic was a symbol of the optimism of the Space Age and the belief that science could make everyday life better, he said. Made from structurally reinforced fiberglass polyester plastic with acrylic, bubblelike windows, the Futuro was designed to be easily moved to a desired site, usually by helicopter. Though originally conceived in Finland, the Donaldsons’ Futuro and most of the others in the U.S. were built by a Philadelphia company under a U.S. license agreement, according to Wayne.

Today, there is a small but devoted community of Futuro enthusiasts, Wayne said, with fans from New Jersey to New Zealand. An informal fan site acts as a central hub, with a global map of locations and a log of recent sales and restorations.

Wayne, 83, said he’s loved space since he was a child; he always gravitated to Sci-Fi stories, like “Flash Gordon” and “Buck Rogers in the 25th Century.” As an adult, he taught a course called “Plastics in Architecture” at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo.

In the late 1970s, Wayne heard that a Futuro was in serious disrepair and about to be destroyed. It had sat for years in a parking lot behind the San Diego Design Center, where it was used for storage. When the design center was sold, the new owners had started the process of demolishing the Futuro, which is about 26 feet in diameter.

Wayne knew he needed to save the Futuro, which had smashed windows and peeling green paint. He said he didn’t recall exactly how much he paid for it. He had no plan for what to do with it; a friend agreed to let him stash it at a San Diego boat yard, where repairs began.

In 2004, Wayne found a roughly 0.5-acre site in the small mountain community of Pine Cove, about 5 miles north of Idyllwild. The land reminded him of the mountain retreat that housed Suuronen’s first Futuro in Finland, he said. He bought it for about $70,000 and made plans to move the Futuro to the site.

Despite Suuronen’s best intentions, relocating the Futuro proved to be quite a challenge. After consulting with experts, Wayne concluded that the structure was too heavy to be lifted by a standard-size helicopter. And airlifting it would require a long list of permits, including approval by the Federal Aviation Administration.

In December of that year, the Futuro was shrink-wrapped and driven about 126 miles from San Diego to Pine Cove on a flatbed truck. It created a spectacle as it was escorted by California Highway Patrol, Wayne said.

“We blocked three lanes of traffic,” he said. “When we finally got up there, it was like we were the Pied Piper. We had about 40 people in cars behind us.” The Futuro was then hoisted by crane above the surrounding trees.

With the home in place, the Donaldsons restored the interior with 1960s flair: It has plastic laminate finishes, linoleum floors and a popcorn ceiling with embedded gold flakes. Most of the materials are original.

Living in a quasi-spaceship comes with its quirks. The one-bedroom, one-bathroom home is accessed by a staircase that swings down from a hatch in the bottom of the structure, Wayne said. Since it’s basically airtight, he said there is never any need to dust, but once a year the exterior needs to be waxed.

Now, Wayne said, his health is failing, and it’s becoming more difficult to maintain the Futuro. He also worries about leaving Laurie, 66, with the burden after he dies. “In case something should happen to me, she’s not going to be strapped with trying to sell it,” he said. “It’s best to try to find a buyer now [who] really appreciates it…. And doesn’t just do an Airbnb or something.”

Idyllwild is known for its pine forests and granite peaks. It has a small downtown, a performing-arts school and an artsy, laid-back vibe, said listing agent Tim McTavish of Desert Sotheby’s International Realty. 

Futuros don’t often come on the market; the few that appear to have sold over the past few decades have brought in between $50,000 and $100,000, though Wayne said they were in poor condition and not livable.

McTavish said he thinks the home is likely to appeal to architecture collectors, museums or foundations.
